r: This introductory course applies knowledge to entrepreneurial ideation: opportunity recognition, generating innovative ideas, and structuring new ventures through workshops and real-world projects. The applied work tasks map to Thinking Creatively and Developing Objectives and Strategies. AI already brainstorms venture concepts, drafts opportunity analyses, and surfaces market gaps competently, but task-exposure research classifies critical-thinking and judgment-heavy work as negatively associated with exposure, and the pedagogical target is the student's own creative problem-framing capacity. There is no licensure, accreditation, or GT-Pathways mandate here (the general-studies field is blank), so no institutional lock protects it; the sole structural protection is its role as prerequisite substrate for CFI 2910. At 24 months, with adoption still partial, the instrumental need to develop ideation judgment is only modestly eroded. Rating Medium, driven by exposed ideation tasks partially offset by the reasoning core.

By 2031 generative tools will fluently produce venture ideas, opportunity scans, and problem-reframing prompts, deepening the tension around whether students must cultivate this themselves. The instrumental case shifts toward the student directing and critically judging AI-generated ideas rather than disappearing: distinguishing a viable opportunity from a plausible-but-wrong one is exactly the jagged-frontier verification problem, where mis-calibrated trust in AI output degrades accuracy. Because no external mandate binds this course, its persistence rests on that residual judgment role and its scaffolding position for feasibility work downstream. Observed-usage data shows business and office tasks are already a prominent, growing share of AI use, which supports continued erosion of the routine ideation the course teaches. The rating holds Medium: material erosion, but the human opportunity-judgment competence remains instrumentally useful across a catalog cycle.

A decade out, in the central case, AI competently performs most idea-generation, opportunity-scanning, and preliminary concept-structuring that this course's knowledge is applied to, and diffusion into entrepreneurship practice is broad. With no licensure or transfer mandate to cap erosion and only light scaffolding value, the instrumental rationale for requiring the course weakens materially, and F1 rises to the High band. The honest hedge: creative problem-framing sits partly in the low-exposure critical-thinking category, so a residue of human judgment in recognizing genuinely novel opportunities plausibly endures, and the ten-year range is wide. But absent any structural brake, the deterministic logic and the trajectory of exposed business tasks both point upward. Rating High, with the caveat that the surviving value is judgment and taste in opportunity selection, not the ideation execution the course currently emphasizes.
CFI 1910.d: This introductory course focuses on creative problem- solving from an entrepreneurial perspective. Content will introduce students to the concepts of creative problem-solving, entrepreneurship, social entrepreneurship, generating innovative ideas, creating entrepreneurial ventures. It highlights practical aspects of opportunity recognition, and new venture creation. The instructor will utilize readings, workshops, guest entrepreneurs, and real-world projects to convey the theoretical underpinnings, as well as the practical realities of solving problems through entrepreneurial principles.

r: The course applies knowledge to social-venture design: business-model generation, reviewing the social-entrepreneurship literature, and using tools to identify opportunities that address societal problems. These tasks map to Analyzing Data or Information and Developing Objectives and Strategies, and they are substantially exposed: AI drafts business-model canvases, synthesizes literature, and frames opportunity hypotheses fluently, with task-exposure research placing writing and routine analysis strongly among positively-associated categories. No licensure, accreditation, or GT-Pathways designation binds the course, so the only structural anchor is weak; it is largely terminal within the minor. At 24 months, partial workplace adoption bounds realized automatability below raw capability, so the instrumental need to learn model generation and opportunity analysis is eroded but not collapsed. Rating Medium: exposed knowledge-work tasks, with near-term diffusion and the human framing of social mission preserving residual necessity.

By 2031 AI will competently generate social-enterprise business models, map stakeholders, and synthesize the field's literature on demand, and GDPval-style evidence already shows leading models approaching human-expert quality on real occupational deliverables. With enterprise adoption broadened in exactly these analytical and writing-heavy tasks, the execution rationale for the course erodes substantially. Crucially, nothing institutional caps that erosion here: there is no transfer mandate or accreditation floor, and the course is not foundational scaffolding for a required sequence. The residual competence is judging whether an AI-proposed social model actually fits a community's need and withstands mission-versus-margin tension, which carries moderate verification burden. The rating rises to High: the applied model-generation and opportunity-analysis tasks are largely AI-performable and deployed, and no structural brake holds the instrumental case down.

In the central 2036 case, AI routinely produces social business models, opportunity assessments, and literature syntheses of the sort this course teaches, with broad diffusion into nonprofit and social-venture practice. Absent any licensure, accreditation, or general-studies mandate, and with the course terminal rather than foundational, there is no mechanism to cap the erosion, so the instrumental case is substantially weakened. The calibrated hedge: social entrepreneurship blends exposed analysis with genuinely human community judgment, stakeholder trust, and ethical weighting of social impact, so a residue of necessity survives around mission definition and legitimacy that AI does not supply to the founder. The ten-year band is wide. But the dominant applied tasks are the automatable analytical and writing ones. Rating High, understanding that surviving value migrates to human mission-judgment rather than the model-generation the course centers.
CFI 1930.d: This course provides an overview of social entrepreneurship, focusing on how it uses innovative business principles to address societal problems. Attention is paid to business model generation, the literature on social entrepreneurship, and the tools used to identify opportunities.

r: The course applies feasibility concepts to determine whether an identified opportunity suits the marketplace, culminating in a comprehensive written venture plan through experiential projects. The applied tasks map to Analyzing Data or Information and Estimating Quantifiable Characteristics, work that task-exposure research places high on the exposure scale, alongside quantitative analysts, and that AI already performs by drafting market analyses, financial projections, and feasibility studies. No licensure, accreditation, or transfer mandate binds the course; its only structural anchor is serving as prerequisite substrate for CFI 3910. At 24 months, capability is real but workplace diffusion is partial, so realized automatability is bounded and the course's own experiential learning still centers the student building the plan. Rating Medium: feasibility and planning tasks are highly exposed, but partial adoption and the human framing of assumptions preserve near-term necessity.

By 2031 AI feasibility tooling will retrieve market data, build financial models, and draft comprehensive venture plans with facility, and GDPval evidence indicates models are approaching expert-level quality on real deliverables of this kind. With enterprise adoption broadened across analytical and writing tasks, the execution rationale for teaching manual feasibility work erodes markedly, and no institutional cap restrains it, since the course carries no mandate and is only lightly foundational. The distinctive residue is judgment: deciding which assumptions are load-bearing and whether a confident-looking projection is actually sound, a moderate verification burden given the cost of a wrong go/no-go call. The rating rises to High, reflecting that the feasibility-analysis and plan-drafting tasks the course's knowledge is applied to are largely AI-performable and increasingly deployed, with only assumption-judgment retained by the human.

In the 2036 central case, AI competently conducts feasibility analysis and produces investor-ready venture plans across most sectors, with deep diffusion into entrepreneurial practice. With no licensure, accreditation, or general-studies brake and only modest scaffolding value, nothing caps the erosion, so the instrumental case for the course is substantially reduced. The calibrated caveat: feasibility ultimately rests on contestable assumptions about a specific market and founder, and the human ability to stress-test an AI-generated projection and own the decision retains value where a wrong assessment is costly and its failure non-obvious. The decade range is genuinely wide. Even so, the analytical and planning execution that the course teaches is squarely in the exposed, deployable band. Rating High, with the surviving competence being critical verification of automated feasibility work rather than its production.
CFI 2910.d: This course determines whether a student's previously identified opportunities are suitable for the marketplace. Students apply feasibility concepts to the wide range of challenges encountered when launching commercial and non-profit ventures. Through experiential learning opportunities, students apply what they learn to develop a comprehensive plan for their own new venture.

r: This upper-division course places students in first-hand, immersive experience working alongside real entrepreneurs, participating as observer and participant in the day-to-day challenges of launching a venture. The instrumental core is embodied and interpersonal: being present in a live startup, building working relationships, and integrating knowledge under real conditions, mapping to Establishing and Maintaining Interpersonal Relationships and Performing for or Working Directly with the Public. Task-exposure research places real-time interpersonal and situated work among the least-exposed categories, and no AI system undergoes the immersion on the student's behalf, which is what dampens the rating. There is no licensure mandate, but embodiment does the protective work: the experiential presence, not a producible deliverable, is the point. At 24 months the instrumental need is essentially intact. Rating Low, anchored by in-person immersion rather than by any institutional lock.

By 2031 AI will handle more of the analytical and documentation tasks a founder faces, and observed-usage data frames such tools as augmenting rather than replacing the operator. That does not touch this course's rationale, which is situated, real-time participation in an actual venture's launch. The experiential, relationship-dependent core resists substitution: an AI cannot sit in the room, absorb the tacit texture of startup decision-making, or build the founder relationships the course is designed to create, and the jagged-frontier caution about mis-calibrated trust makes on-the-ground human judgment more valuable, not less. With no external mandate but strong embodiment, the instrumental case holds. The rating stays Low: the surrounding entrepreneurial toolset automates, but the immersive learning-by-doing that the course delivers is not something AI performs for the student across this horizon.

Even in an aggressive 2036 scenario where AI runs much of the routine operational and analytical work of new ventures, the specific thing this course provides, embodied immersion alongside practicing entrepreneurs and the interpersonal judgment formed in a live launch, is not a task AI executes on the learner's behalf. Embodiment keeps direct substitution low regardless of capability, and there is no institutional lock doing the work here; the protection is intrinsic to experiential presence. The honest hedge is that more of what the student observes founders doing may itself be AI-mediated by 2036, subtly changing what the immersion teaches, but not whether being immersed remains necessary. The rating holds Low with medium confidence: the applied core is situated human participation, categorically distinct from the digital knowledge-work that AI increasingly performs.
CFI 3910.d: This course provides first-hand experience working alongside entrepreneurs to facilitate the launch of student conceived business plans. The goal is to enable students to work with commercial and social/non-profit entrepreneurs to gain experience with the multiple facets of entrepreneurship. This course serves two main learning objectives. First, it provides the student with the opportunity to execute an entrepreneurial project which will encourage the integration of your knowledge. Second, it gives the student first hand exposure to the entrepreneurial process in order to understand the challenges associated with it. Coursework on fundamental business concepts and on developing and executing a business plan are excellent foundations for entrepreneurs, but they are different from facing the day-to-day challenges in a start-up, In this course, the student is immersed as an observer and participant of the entrepreneurial process.

r: A continuation of CFI 3910, this course again immerses the student as observer and participant in an actual venture launch, executing an entrepreneurial project alongside real entrepreneurs to integrate prior coursework under live conditions. The applied core is the same embodied, interpersonal participation, mapping to Establishing and Maintaining Interpersonal Relationships and Coordinating the Work and Activities of Others, which task-exposure research classifies as low-exposure situated work. No AI substitutes for the student being present in the startup, so embodiment dampens the rating and there is no institutional mandate carrying it. At 24 months the instrumental need for hands-on immersion is intact; the value is the lived experience, not a deliverable an AI could produce. Rating Low, held by real-time presence rather than any licensure or accreditation floor, consistent with the treatment of the first course in the sequence.

By 2031 the analytical and administrative scaffolding around a startup will be heavily AI-assisted, and observed-usage patterns indicate augmentation of operators rather than replacement. This leaves the experiential rationale of the course untouched: continued first-hand participation in launching a venture, forming the founder relationships and situational judgment that only presence produces. Verification concerns reinforce the point; where AI proposes actions of uneven quality, a human embedded in the venture is needed to judge them, exactly the jagged-frontier condition. With no external mandate but strong embodiment and a terminal position in the minor, the instrumental case rests entirely on situated learning that AI does not perform for the student. The rating stays Low: the venture's tooling gets more automated, but the immersive apprenticeship this course delivers does not become AI-substitutable across a catalog cycle.

In the central 2036 case, AI will perform much of the operational and analytical labor of running a new venture, and more of what founders do day-to-day may be AI-mediated. Yet the pedagogical function here, the student personally participating in and learning from a live launch, remains categorically outside what AI executes on the learner's behalf; embodiment and real-time interpersonal judgment are the whole point. There is no institutional lock; the protection is intrinsic. The calibrated caveat is that the content of what students observe will shift as ventures automate, changing the texture of the apprenticeship without removing the need to serve it. The rating holds Low with medium confidence: even amid broad automation of entrepreneurial knowledge-work, situated experiential participation is the least-substitutable form of the discipline's learning.
CFI 3920.d: This course is a continuation of CFI 3910 and provides first-hand experience working alongside entrepreneurs and facilitating the launch of student conceived business plans. This course serves two main learning objectives. First, it provides the student with the opportunity to execute an entrepreneurial project which will encourage the integration of the student's knowledge. Second, it gives the student first hand exposure to the entrepreneurial process in order to understand the challenges associated with it. In this course, the student is immersed as an observer and participant of the entrepreneurial process.

r: The course applies knowledge to promoting a new venture through bootstrapped, guerrilla tactics: minimedia, positioning, and preparing a small-business promotional budget. These tasks map to Selling or Influencing Others, Communicating with Persons Outside the Organization, and Thinking Creatively, and they are among the most-exposed in the evidence base, PR and marketing writing rank high in task-exposure research, and controlled studies show large time-and-quality gains on professional writing with AI assistance. AI already drafts positioning statements, ad copy, and promotional plans competently. No licensure, accreditation, or GT-Pathways designation binds the course, and it is terminal rather than foundational, so nothing structural caps erosion. At 24 months, partial workplace adoption bounds realized automatability, so the instrumental need is materially but not fully eroded. Rating Medium: highly exposed promotional tasks tempered only by near-term diffusion limits.

By 2031 AI will fluently generate positioning, guerrilla-marketing campaigns, minimedia content, and promotional budgets, and GDPval-type evidence shows models approaching expert quality on real marketing deliverables. Enterprise adoption in writing-and-marketing tasks is already high and broadening, so the execution rationale for teaching students to produce promotional materials themselves erodes sharply. With no institutional mandate and no foundational role, nothing restrains that erosion. The residual competence is strategic judgment, choosing positioning that actually differentiates and reading whether a campaign lands, plus the moderate verification burden of catching an off-brand or misleading AI draft. The rating rises to High: the promotional content-generation and budgeting tasks the course's knowledge is applied to are largely AI-performable and deployed, with only campaign strategy and brand judgment retained by the human, insufficient to hold the rating down.

In the 2036 central case, AI competently produces the full promotional stack, positioning, creative, media planning, and budgets, for small ventures, with deep diffusion into marketing practice. With no licensure, accreditation, or transfer brake and a terminal curricular position, there is nothing to cap the erosion, so the instrumental case for the course is substantially reduced. The calibrated hedge: promotion still rewards human taste, brand intuition, and knowing a specific audience, so a residue of strategic direction survives that AI does not supply to the founder, and the decade range is wide. But the dominant applied tasks, generating and budgeting promotional campaigns, are precisely the writing-and-influence work the evidence flags as most exposed. Rating High, with surviving value migrating to strategic and brand judgment over the content production the course currently teaches.
CFI 3930.d: The purpose of this course is to present to the entrepreneur the fundamental theories of promoting a new business or social enterprise. Building from the start-up strategy of bootstrapping, students will learn vital aspects of guerrilla tactics such as minimedia, positioning, and preparing a small business promotional budget.

r: The course gives students tools to turn artistic practice into a business: opening and operating galleries, working the festival circuit and retail, and using alternative channels such as online direct sales and online representation. The applied knowledge tasks, marketing, pricing, channel setup, and small-business operations, map to Selling or Influencing Others and Developing Objectives and Strategies, and are substantially exposed; AI drafts e-commerce listings, pricing strategies, and outreach, with productivity research showing the largest uplift accrues to lower-skill or novice operators, which describes artists new to business. Some tasks (running a physical gallery, festival booths) are embodied, but the course's transferable knowledge is business-planning and digital-channel work. No licensure, accreditation, or transfer mandate binds it, and it is terminal. At 24 months, partial adoption limits realized automatability. Rating Medium: exposed business-of-art tasks, with near-term diffusion and some in-person retail residue.

By 2031 AI will competently handle the online-storefront setup, listing copy, pricing guidance, audience outreach, and administrative operations that make up much of the art-business toolkit, and observed-usage data shows business and office tasks are a large, growing share of AI use. Enterprise diffusion into small-business commerce broadens the realized automation, and with no institutional cap and no foundational role, the erosion is unrestrained. The residual value is genuinely human, the artist's own creative work and the in-person relationships of gallery and festival selling, but those are not the transferable business knowledge the course primarily teaches. The rating rises to High: the marketing, channel-management, and administrative tasks the course's knowledge is applied to are largely AI-performable and deployed by this horizon, leaving mainly embodied retail presence, which is not enough to hold the instrumental case down.

In the 2036 central case, AI runs most of the digital business operations of an art practice, storefronts, pricing, promotion, customer communication, and administration, with broad diffusion among independent creators. With no licensure, accreditation, or general-studies brake and a terminal position, nothing caps the erosion, so the instrumental case for the business-skills content is substantially reduced. The calibrated caveat: selling art still depends on in-person relationships at galleries and festivals and on the artist's irreplaceable creative output, so an embodied and relational residue endures that AI does not perform for the artist, and the decade band is wide. But the course's transferable knowledge is the automatable business-and-marketing layer. Rating High, with surviving necessity concentrated in the physical selling contexts and creative work rather than the business administration the course teaches.
CFI 3940.d: The purpose of this course is to give students the tools, techniques and resources to turn their passion for art into a thriving business. Students will learn how open and operate galleries, own a business on the festival circuit, and retail, as well as alternative distribution channels such as online direct sales, direct sales, business to business and online galleries/representation. Upon completion of the course, each student will have the basics to move forward with building a successful art business.

r: This is a supervised internship in a for-profit or nonprofit enterprise, with the student performing real work on the job under a professional's oversight. The instrumental core is definitionally embodied and situated: showing up in a workplace, doing entrepreneurial work under supervision, and building professional relationships, mapping to Establishing and Maintaining Interpersonal Relationships and situated on-the-job activity. Task-exposure research places such real-time, in-person work among the least-exposed categories, and no AI system serves the internship on the student's behalf, which drives the low rating through embodiment. There is no licensure mandate; the protection is intrinsic to the experiential form, and the course is terminal and non-foundational. At 24 months the instrumental need for supervised workplace experience is fully intact. Rating Low, anchored by the irreducibly in-person, real-work nature of an internship rather than any institutional floor.

By 2031 AI will be embedded in the workflows of the host organizations, and observed-usage data frames it as augmenting workers rather than replacing the human on the job. That does not touch the internship's rationale, which is the student personally accumulating supervised professional experience, judgment, and workplace relationships that only presence produces. Diffusion of AI into firms continues to lag capability, and even a heavily AI-assisted workplace still requires the intern to be there doing and learning the work. With no external mandate but maximal embodiment, the instrumental case is untouched. The rating stays Low: the tools the intern uses on the job get more capable, but the experiential, real-time professional immersion the course requires is not a task AI performs for the student across this horizon, and no structural feature pushes it upward.

Even in an aggressive 2036 scenario where AI performs much routine knowledge-work inside host organizations, an internship's function, situated, supervised, real-world professional experience, is not something AI executes on the learner's behalf. Embodiment and in-person presence keep substitution at floor regardless of capability, and there is no institutional lock in play; the protection is inherent to the experiential design. The honest hedge is that the content of the work an intern does will itself be more AI-mediated by 2036, changing what the internship teaches, but not whether being in the workplace remains necessary to learn it. The rating holds Low with high confidence: across every horizon, supervised on-the-job experience is the least AI-substitutable element of the curriculum, categorically distinct from the digital tasks automation increasingly absorbs.
CFI 3980.d: This course provides an internship experience in a for- profit or non-profit enterprise supervised by professionals with on- the-job experience in the field of entrepreneurship.
